HEADLINE: Developers rush to flip sites as values peak
INTRO: As values peak, a growing number of east coast development sites are being listed for sale with those carrying a development permit attracting premium pricing.
TEXT:
As values peak, a growing number of east coast development sites are being listed for sale with those carrying a development permit attracting premium pricing.

Sydney-based Alpha Fund has listed a DA-approved site in Sydney's Waterloo, near the future new township of Green Square.

The fund purchased the 1436-square-metre site at 713-717 Elizabeth Street in 2013 for $12.5 million and spent the last two years pursuing a development application (DA) permit for a four-storey apartment block with 36 units and a communal rooftop terrace with views of the Sydney CBD. One third of the apartments have already been sold off the plan.

In Brisbane, Metro Property Development is marketing its Montpelier Road site in the inner north eastern suburb of Bowen Hills, which has a DA permit under way and for which it paid about $25 million in late 2014. Deloitte Real Estate's James Walsh and Ray White's Rick Bird are marketing the site, which can yield 509 apartments across five eight-storey towers.

"Two years ago, there wasn't a premium on sites with a DA, people were happy to wait and get their DA. It was like the gold rush, people were waiting for things to go up in value," JLL's Sam Brewer who is marketing the Waterloo site, said. "But now the market has stabilised."

The steady market has produced two kinds of site sellers - developers and investors who acquired sites a few years ago, added value to them with a DA and are now crystallising risk-free profits in lieu of development, and developers who have found themselves "road-blocked".

Road-blocked developers were those who were unable to get finance, construction labour or required pre-sales of apartments or houses, Colliers International Head of Residential in North Sydney Ryan Bennetts said. Together these two groups make up 30 per cent of the market, with the majority being road-blocked developers.

"These are the ones who have come unstuck," he said.

"Among them are those who call themselves developers ... but banks do not recognise them.

"Now that the market has shifted buyers are going to the big established developers."

The rest of the market is still made up of "usual" site sales - private owners selling to developers. Despite the changes, prices of sites remained high and at a premium. No one is losing money, not even in broader western Sydney where speculations of a housing crash are rife, CBRE's Alex Mirzaian said.

"I have 100 inquiries for five sites, raw or with DA," he said. "Yes, apartment sales are slowing, you could sell 200 in one weekend in the past, now it's about 30 to 40.

"And it is true that there is a certain point when developers had bought their sites for too much... the whole feasibility of the site is then thrown out of the window."

But there is still a rush of developers who are looking for ready-to-build sites, all the agents confirmed.

New Chinese entrants such as China Overseas Holdings and Macrolink fuel demand for sites. Australia's biggest developer Meriton, after buying its first 2016 site in Mascot in Sydney's south for $67 million, is still looking for more large raw and DA-approved sites 15 to 20 kilometres from the Sydney CBD.

In the steadier Melbourne market, while there is not as much site flipping, there is uncertainty about the changes in planning, CBRE director Mark Wizel said.

Qualitas managing director Andrew Schwartz told The Australian Financial Review earlier this month the real estate financier would steer clear of investing in development sites, which he said were a no-go zone at current pricing levels.

HEADLINE: Citibank closes branches
INTRO: Citibank is paring its branch presence in Australia by about half, as the major banks also reassess their footprints, sources told Street Talk.
TEXT:
Citibank is paring its branch presence in Australia by about half, as the major banks also reassess their footprints, sources told Street Talk.

Citi is preparing to shut Sydney branches in Castle Hill, Chatswood and Chinatown in late March. In the second quarter, it plans to close Sydney's Wynyard and Queen Victoria Building branches as well as its Little Bourke branch in Melbourne.

Some of those outlets are not full-service and are known as cashless or compact branches.

A Citi spokesman said the bank would continue to operate in the major cities of Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane and Perth, with one flagship branch in each, and a further three branches in Sydney.

He added that more than 80 per cent of Citi's customer acquisitions were now digital.

HEADLINE: APN taps Credit Suisse on sell-off of newspapers
INTRO: APN News & Media has Credit Suisse in its corner as it goes about trying to find a buyer for its regional newspapers business, as revealed by Street Talk on Sunday.
TEXT:
APN News & Media has Credit Suisse in its corner as it goes about trying to find a buyer for its regional newspapers business, as revealed by Street Talk on Sunday.

This column understands Credit Suisse's bankers - who know APN's shareholder register well after selling a 30 per cent stake in the company this time last year - have been hired to progress initial interest garnered by chief executive Ciaran Davis' team.

News Corp shapes as the most likely buyer. The company already has a 14.99 per cent stake in APN and knows its Australian Regional Media arm well, having spoken previously about a potential deal.

But News shareholders are also reeling from a decline in print media earnings and you would have to wonder what minority shareholders, at least, would make of another print investment.

It's also Credit Suisse's job to ensure APN has more than one party at the negotiating table. No doubt they will highlight Warren Buffett's enthusiasm for local newspapers. The pitch is all about finding a buyer willing to invest in the digital side of the business. Davis and his team would prefer to focus on radio and outdoor media.

The APN unit up for sale had $18.4 million in earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation in the year to December 31, which was down 26.6 per cent on the previous corresponding period.

APN also took a $50 million write-down on the unit in the year, after a handful of big national advertisers said they would be leaving regional media late last year.

Analysts expect the business may be worth up to $100 million.

HEADLINE: MetLife interest heats up Macquarie life auction
INTRO: Life insurance deals look set to accelerate in the domestic market as Macquarie Group prepares to field final bids for its life unit this week.
TEXT:
Life insurance deals look set to accelerate in the domestic market as Macquarie Group prepares to field final bids for its life unit this week.

Street Talk can reveal that MetLife, the largest US life insurer, is preparing to lob a final bid for the division.

Macquarie is understood to be keen to get an outcome on the sale ahead of its March 31 year end. A potential transaction would not come as a surprise for life insurance industry observers. Last year, National Australia Bank sold a chunk of its MLC life business to Japanese company Nippon Life.

A play by MetLife would help propel it to a stronger position in Australia's $14 billion life insurance market. According to figures from Credit Suisse, MetLife controls 4 per cent of the market, compared with Macquarie's 1 per cent.

Buying Macquarie's book would give MetLife the firepower to compete on a more even footing with Suncorp, which has market share of 5 per cent. TAL, AMP, AIA, MLC and CommInsure number among Australia's five biggest life insurers. Spokespersons for Macquarie and MetLife declined to comment on the life insurance sale process.

This column revealed in December that Macquarie was considering a sale of the division.

It has zero exposure to the profit-hit group risk sector which sells life insurance policies through superannuation funds.

Following the NAB transaction, management meetings were held late last year on Macquarie's life unit. It distributes policies through financial advisers.

A tilt by MetLife makes sense as it knows the local market well. Last year the company signed an agreement with Yellow Brick Road to sell mortgage insurance ahead of the listed wealth group's plan to offer life and income protection products.

Elsewhere in insurance, advisers Macquarie Capital and Goldman Sachs are understood to have distributed sale documents for a stake in insurance reseller Greenstone.

The company, which is majority owned by The Enthoven Family Trust and serial entrepreneur Gavin Donnelly, wants to sell 40 per cent of the business through a trade sale after shelving a float in 2015.

Finally, on the potential listing of financial planning business StatePlus, documents will be submitted and bankers will on Friday pitch for a second joint lead manager role. Earlier this month, as foreshadowed by this column, Macquarie went to rival investment banks to progress the float option of the dual-track process.

HEADLINE: Sponsors weigh ride on Ardent merry-go-round
INTRO: When the private equity sector meets in Sydney this week at Asian Venture Capital Journal's Private Equity and Venture Forum, the focus is likely to be on buying rather than selling.
TEXT:
When the private equity sector meets in Sydney this week at Asian Venture Capital Journal's Private Equity and Venture Forum, the focus is likely to be on buying rather than selling.

Private equity firms are tipped to be ready to spend some $5.5 billion in capital in 2016, as acquisitions replace exits as the sector's main game.

Not only are the private equity firms themselves ready to spend, but in the wake of reporting season, investment banks have subtly started shopping around some companies that had less than sparkling first-half results.

One company that could fit the bill is theme park, gym, ten pin bowling and video arcade operator Ardent Leisure.

The group posted a 20 per cent increase in half-year net profit to $22.6 million on February 18, driven mainly by the expansion in its United States-based Main Event arm.

But investors were less than impressed, sending its shares down to $1.75, the lowest since July 2013.

While the US division is now on an equal footing with the group's theme park division in terms of earnings contribution, some in the market reckon that Ardent isn't the natural owner of the business.

And with Ardent also considered a potential seller of its DreamWorld theme park to Chinese giant Wanda, a break-up play could emerge as an option.

With a market capitalisation of about $867 million (just above fellow sponsor target Greencross), it's a size that would be digestible for private equity.

But who is ready to jump on the rollercoaster? It's understood Citi would be drafted in should a sponsor or strategic buyer emerge from the sidelines.

Street Talk can also reveal Ardent has hired Market Eye, a specialist investor and media relations advisory firm, to talk with investors in the coming weeks about their views on the company's management, strategy and performance.

It's understood this is considered an offensive move from Ardent rather than a defensive one - these conversations are designed to give management the ammunition to remind investors of why the stock is undervalued.

Ardent's shareholders may well have some more pointed suggestions about the company's future.

HEADLINE: Woolworths SA takes a peep at Harris Farm
INTRO: The deck chairs are constantly shifting in the gourmet food sector and this year is no different. Street Talk can reveal South Africa's Woolworths Holdings, which is seeking to bolster its Australian food business, has run a ruler over Harris Farm Markets.
TEXT:
The deck chairs are constantly shifting in the gourmet food sector and this year is no different. Street Talk can reveal South Africa's Woolworths Holdings, which is seeking to bolster its Australian food business, has run a ruler over Harris Farm Markets.

Harris Farm has 24 stores around NSW and was founded by David and Cathy Harris. Woolworths SA and Harris Farm declined to comment on the approach.

The local company is, however, no stranger to fielding inbound interest, but it remains unclear whether the family are sellers.

Last year, this column revealed Harris Farm received approaches from trade and private equity buyers. The company itself is also understood to be evaluating its own acquisitions and is in the throes of assessing a potential purchase of Sydney-based Norton Street Grocer.

It comes as embattled local supermarket giant Woolworths retreats from its gourmet food offering, Thomas Dux, to focus on improving group results.

David Jones and Woolworths SA last year said their immediate priority was fixing the existing food offer, including updating David Jones' food halls and possibly adding cafes and restaurants to key stores. That would come before any stand-alone food stores.

Buying Harris Farm, or a stake in the company, would provide a neater inroad into the gourmet food segment. Australia's entire grocery market is worth $90 billion and has been targeted by offshore players, including Germany's ALDI.

John Dixon, the British retail veteran lured to Australia to revitalise David Jones, has already thrown down the gauntlet to Woolworths and Coles, saying supermarket shopping has become old-fashioned and people want more inspiration and less choice.

Elsewhere, indicative bids for a 50.4 per cent stake in electricity distribution company Ausgrid are due on Monday and the list of bidders looks relatively limited.

Street Talk understands State Grid Corporation of China put the final touches on its offer to submit to the NSW government and its advisers over the weekend. Cheung Kong Infrastructure, after missing out on acquiring London City Airport, was also preparing to lob a bid.

But questions are being raised about whether the Qatar Investment Authority-China Southern Power group will forge ahead with an offer, given the large cheque required. Added to that uncertainty is whether two Chinese state firms would be granted permission to make it through to Ausgrid's final furlong.

HEADLINE: Super union could 'lock up the nation'
INTRO: The militant maritime and construction unions will consider mergers with unions representing tens of thousands of road transport, aviation and rail workers, potentially creating a new super union that business warned could "lock up the nation".
TEXT:
The militant maritime and construction unions will consider mergers with unions representing tens of thousands of road transport, aviation and rail workers, potentially creating a new super union that business warned could "lock up the nation".

Maritime Union of Australia national secretary Paddy Crumlin said the MUA's proposed merger with the Construction, Forestry, Mining and Energy Union was "not a one-off" and he was willing to have amalgamation talks with the Transport Workers Union, the Rail, Tram and Bus Union and the Australian Workers' Union.

"I am of the view, and our national council is generally of the view, that the union movement needs to go into the next stage of restructuring," he told The Australian Financial Review.

Mr Crumlin said the 14,000-member MUA's alliance with the TWU (90,000 members) and RTBU (35,000 members) through the Australian Transport Union Federation "could easily translate into the next stage of trade union consolidation on the basis of the trust and leadership generated by our effective campaigning".

He said the MUA also had a good relationship with the AWU (93,000 members). "We don't want to rule anything out, including the AWU, as much as that would horrify them that I said it," he said.

The comments reflect the union movement's increasing examination of mergers in the face of record low union membership. The Turnbull government and industry groups expressed concern on Sunday that the mergers would result in increased militancy and unlawful industrial action.

Federal Employment Minister Michaelia Cash said on Sunday the "significantly disturbing history" of the CFMEU and the MUA meant their merger "represents a very real threat to jobs, productivity and the Australian economy".

"Both unions have a record of disregard for the economic damage they inflict on their own industries," she said. "Their combined effect will have the potential to put at risk other industries as well."

Master Builders Australia chief executive Wilhelm Harnisch said on Sunday the construction industry was concerned the merger would result in "double the militancy".

"Both unions have shown a total disregard for the law," Mr Harnisch said. "They disregard court orders; they disregard orders from the Fair Work Commission. They seem to wear it as a badge of honour.

"There is potential for them to lock up the nation industrially. That is not hyperbole, and their talk now of a merger with unions like the TWU only adds to the fear that such a massive union could have the potential to basically lock up the country."

In interviews with the Financial Review, CFMEU national secretary Michael O'Connor and Mr Crumlin rejected the criticism, and denied their proposed marriage was driven by a desire to enhance their influence in the Labor Party.

Delegates to the MUA's national conference will vote this week on whether to authorise the union's leadership to start formal negotiations with the CFMEU about the conditions for their proposed merger.

Mr Crumlin revealed any merger with the 110,000-member CFMEU might not be finalised until 2017, as it would be conditional on support by a plebiscite of the MUA's members.

He dismissed the industry group complaints, insisting the merger has been driven by the aggressive ideologically driven tactics of the Coalition.

"It's not a conspiracy, a Trojan horse for industrial leverage or power. It's just a commonsense thing in the face of a brutal neo-conservative offensive," he said.

Mr O'Connor said the CFMEU, which is separately negotiating a merger with the Textile, Clothing and Footwear Union of Australia, shared a "lot of common values" with the MUA.

"The MUA brings a lot to the table," he said. "The great tradition and history of being a union that really fights hard to protect its members, the members' families and their communities."

TWU national secretary Tony Sheldon said Mr Crumlin had been asked to address the TWU national committee of management "to discuss his views on greater co-operation". He said the TWU, the MUA and RTBU had "excellent working relations".

AWU national secretary Scott McDine said his union had a history of mergers but had not held any amalgamation discussions with the MUA. He said he expected the union movement's structure to change substantially over the next decade.

HEADLINE: G20 rejects global stimulus push
INTRO: Finance ministers from 20 of the world's largest economies have left a meeting in Shanghai without a plan to boost growth, as Australian Treasurer Scott Morrison and others rejected the need for co-ordinated global stimulus.
TEXT:
Finance ministers from 20 of the world's largest economies have left a meeting in Shanghai without a plan to boost growth, as Australian Treasurer Scott Morrison and others rejected the need for co-ordinated global stimulus.

The communique, issued on Saturday night, contained few initiatives, despite the International Monetary Fund declaring before the meeting "bold multilateral actions" and a more co-ordinated policy response were needed to boost the world economy.

"They should go bold, they should go broad and they should go together," IMF managing director Christine Lagarde said before the meeting.

Instead, finance ministers and central bank governors of the so-called Group of 20 agreed to more of the same in their eight-page statement.

"While conscious of the strong economic headwinds facing all economies, the G20 restated its commitment to use all available policy levers to drive growth," Mr Morrison said on Sunday after the meeting had ended.

"There was also a sober recognition that, as short-term measures designed merely to bring forward demand, fiscal and monetary stimulus were not a substitute for implementing the necessary structural reforms in our economies to boost productivity and drive growth over the media to longer term," he said of the tone of the Shanghai gathering.

Mr Morrison said he was looking forward to the implementation of reforms that the G20 had already started, referencing a push to crack down on multinational tax avoidance.

"Our contributions at the G20 focused on the need to appreciate the opportunities for growth afforded by innovation and to focus on policies that would unlock private-sector demand and encourage private sector investment," he said.

His call was echoed by German Finance Minister Wolfgang Schauble, who said the hard work of structural reform must be the focus of each country.

"Fiscal as well as monetary policies have reached their limits," he said. "If you want the real economy to grow there are no shortcuts which avoid reforms. Talking about further stimulus just distracts from the real tasks at hand."

Mr Morrison said he backed the concerns of the German government prior to the meeting and relayed those comments in his bilateral meeting with Mr Schauble.

However, some countries are expected to boost government spending to lift growth, including China, with its finance officials flagging an increase in the fiscal deficit, which was 2.3 per cent of gross domestic product last year. An announcement is expected this Saturday as China's National People's Congress is held in Beijing.

Finance Minister Lou Jiwei said monetary policy would likely remain loose, but greater government spending was also needed.

"Monetary policy will probably have to be kept appropriately loose, even though people have realised that its role cannot replace fiscal policy," said Mr Lou.

The G20 communique noted this lack of agreement among members. "We agree we need to do more to achieve our common objective for global growth," it said.

"The global recovery continues, but it remains uneven and falls short of our ambition for strong, sustainable and balance growth."

The one initiative from the meeting was an agreement that members would inform each other of major changes in currency policies.

This followed China's surprise move last August to devalue the yuan and change the way it sets the exchange rate, sparking turmoil on global equity and currency markets.

Rather than bold initiatives, the meeting in Shanghai may be remembered for the United States regaining its confidence at a time when its challenger, China, was on the defensive.

In a statement after the meeting, US Treasury Secretary Jacob Lew said the American economy was one of the few bright spots around the world, having added 14 million new jobs over 71 months, which had seen unemployment drop below 5 per cent.

"We need to redouble our efforts to boost global demand, rather than relying on the United States as the consumer of last resort," said Mr Lew.

He also took aim at China, saying it needed to hasten reform, better communicate its policies and not resort to competitive devaluation of its currency.

"The United States believes that China has the necessary tools, including through fiscal policies, to support household demand and succeed in its economic transition," he said. "The United States continues to underscore the importance of China carrying out this transition in an orderly and transparent manner."

This followed China's central bank governor mounting a strong defence of the world's second-biggest economy on Friday.

Zhou Xiaochuan, governor of the People's Bank of China, said the economy would continue to grow at a "moderate to high pace" and contribute to global growth at a rate that is comparable with its share in the global economy.

He said China's economic activity was showing positive signs with strong credit growth in January and robust retail sales during the Chinese New Year holiday. The central bank had room to cut interest rates and the government planned to increase spending to head off any sharp slowdown.

'China still has some monetary policy space and multiple policy instruments to address possible downside risks," he said.

HEADLINE: Tax policy and poll to come early
INTRO: The Turnbull government is working towards an early-April tax statement that will outline plans for income tax cuts funded primarily by pruning superannuation tax concessions, with some changes to negative gearing and workplace expenses.
TEXT:
The Turnbull government is working towards an early-April tax statement that will outline plans for income tax cuts funded primarily by pruning superannuation tax concessions, with some changes to negative gearing and workplace expenses.

Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull is seeking to bed down the tax issue, as a July double-dissolution election becomes an increasing certainty.

Bracing for further political attack on its missing tax agenda in Parliament this week, the PM said on Sunday the government would not be rushed into making changes that have already been under development for some months.

"The government's approach is to work carefully through all the elements in the tax system and assess how we can make changes that will be both fair and provide greater incentives to work, save and invest," he told The Australian Financial Review.

"That work will be completed shortly and the results will be announced in the lead-up to the budget.

"When you rush changes to the tax system you make mistakes. We have seen this approach to tax policy from Labor before. Australia can not afford reckless and piecemeal changes that would hurt confidence, discourage investment and damage the economy."

However, there is a widespread recognition within the government now that it left the public tax debate unoccupied for too long and that it has no choice but to deliver a comprehensive statement before the May 10 budget.

Work on the tax plan has accelerated and intensified in the past week and is expected to be considered by the expenditure review committee of cabinet this week. There is only more sitting week of Parliament after this week, beginning on March 14, and signals on Sunday were that the government was not planning to release its tax plans by then, which means the release is likely to then be slotted in after the political calendar slows down over Easter.

Strategists want to steady and lock in not just the government's political line on tax, but also its wider message as the push towards the election campaign intensifies.

They argue that the government must highlight its other policy proposals, like last week's defence white paper, to show that it has been getting on with governing - and indeed clearing backlogs left over from the Abbott era - as well as entrench the jobs and growth themes that will be the centrepiece of the federal budget.

Reform of the Senate, and the potential implications of that for running the government and Parliament more smoothly, is inevitably pushing the Coalition towards a double-dissolution election as a vehicle to "clear out" the existing Senate and also bring home its point about trying to improve governance in Canberra.

Spurring on Mr Turnbull's need to hasten slowly was a long discussion on tax at last Monday's cabinet meeting, which highlighted that the need to get the tax package and its supporting political arguments right will start with the cabinet itself.

Sources say cabinet ministers made clear they wanted a "pretty forensic examination of the tax changes being proposed" amid backbench agitation against a mooted crackdown on negative gearing.

"There were pretty strong views around the table on the direction and benefits of tax reform", they said, and the first task facing Mr Turnbull and Treasurer Scott Morrison would be to persuade their cabinet colleagues about the efficacy of their plans.

The need for the statement to be comprehensive, rather than reflect earlier plans to simply outline some reform options on, say, super, comes from a political reading that, after the past few weeks, "you don't want to be having your salami sliced one piece at a time, which is what has been happening since the decision to not commit to a GST, and individual issues like negative gearing have come each day".

An extensive cabinet, then party room, discussion would also honour Mr Turnbull's repeated commitments to follow proper process, they said.

The government's decision to not proceed with a 15 per cent GST, combined with an initially positive reception to Labor's plans to limit negative gearing to new housing, has put the Turnbull government on the back foot on tax, and opened the floodgates to criticism internally, as well as from voters already suffering a let-down from their high expectations of policy change after Mr Turnbull replaced Tony Abbott as prime minister.

Mr Turnbull continues to insist that Labor has not thought through the impact of its negative gearing proposals on the property market, nor their equity considerations.

"Labor's reckless and ill-considered changes to prohibit negative gearing on existing residential property and massively increase capital gains tax on all investments are a good example of the dangers of making tax policy on the run," he said on Sunday.

"Australians know that if you take away a third of the crowd at an auction the price you get for your house will be lower.

"They know that increasing the tax on investment gains will only discourage people from investing - right at the time when we need more investment as we transition from the mining boom."

By contrast, he said, the government would work through its proposals carefully and methodically.

Advice about what the government should do on tax is coming from all quarters, including former prime minister John Howard, who at the weekend urged the government to be careful about changing negative gearing arrangements.

"There are a lot of modest-income people who accumulate some money and then negatively gear a property, particularly [those] who don't want to invest in the share market," Mr Howard said.

Mr Turnbull said on Sunday: "It is very important to treat any changes to the tax system very carefully indeed and indeed I had a long chat with John [Howard] about negative gearing and other aspects of tax only yesterday, in fact, a long chat.

"He's obviously a great source of advice. You can see that what Labor has done with their proposed changes will have a very negative impact on housing values.

"It's the biggest single asset class in Australia.

"It's where most Australian families have most of their net worth, their wealth, tied up and to administer such a big shock to such an important asset class at a time when the economy is going through a transition, from a mining construction boom, we're travelling well but it is a turbulent world out there in terms of the global economy. We understand that and we're going through a period of transition.

"Confidence is everything, absolutely everything, and to administer such a big shock to the single biggest asset class is very reckless, so what John says about being careful with tax policy is absolutely right. That's why we are taking the time to analyse these things, these issues very carefully and Labor clearly did not. They thought they would get political credit for a big announcement but without thinking through the consequences of what they've done."

To an observation from a journalist that his comments suggested he was ruling out changes to negative gearing, Mr Turnbull said: "It sounds like I'm doing my job as Prime Minister looking at these issues very, very carefully.

"That's what Australians expect me to do and frankly it is what they expect would-be prime ministers like Mr Shorten to do but he has not done that. What he's proposing will have a very negative impact on housing values and let's face it, that's what they want to do. They want Australian homes to fall in value and they say this is good because it will make them more affordable but it undermines the financial situation, the wealth and hence the confidence of most Australian families.

"As John Howard was saying, the last time the abolition of negative gearing was tried by the Labor Party and they did in fact legislate it, it was quickly reversed because of its negative impact on the housing and in particular the rental market.

"So Howard's advice, look at these things carefully and absolutely, that's exactly what I am doing.

"Pity Labor didn't."
